topic: The Fundamental Connection: Bridging Derivatives and Integrals
target_audience: High school seniors or first-year university students

sections.title: Introduction: The Inverse Twins
lecture_lines: Differentiation and integration are inverse operations.
They are like addition and subtraction for functions.
Today, we bridge these two mathematical worlds.
animations: Fade in a 'Function Machine' icon [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/machine.svg] (#FFFFFF) in center.
Show a shape being sliced into thin vertical strips (#00FF00) by a 'Derivative Lever' (#FFD700).
Show the strips being glued back into the original shape (#00FF00) by an 'Integration Lever' (#1E90FF).

sections.title: Prerequisite Refresh: Slope vs. Area
lecture_lines: Derivatives measure the instantaneous slope of a curve.
Integrals calculate the accumulated area under a curve.
These concepts seem distinct but are deeply linked.
animations: Show a speedometer [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/speedometer.svg] with a needle (#FF0000) moving to represent rate.
Show a curve f(x) (#FFFFFF) with a growing shaded area (#FFFF00) beneath it.
Highlight the label 'Slope' (#FF0000) and 'Area' (#FFFF00) side-by-side.

sections.title: The Dynamic Area Function
lecture_lines: Let's define a function that tracks accumulated area.
A(x) starts at a fixed point a.
It ends at a moving variable point x.
As x moves right, the area shield grows.
This creates a new function representing total area.
animations: Draw a white curve (#FFFFFF) on a black background, marking the starting point 'a' with a shield icon [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/shield.svg].
Shade the region from a fixed 'a' to moving 'x' (#00FFFF).
Show 'x' sliding right, causing the cyan area to expand.
Display the label 'A(x)' (#00FFFF) increasing as 'x' moves.

sections.title: The 'Aha!' Moment: The Rate of Area Growth
lecture_lines: How fast does this area function A(x) change?
Move x by a tiny amount called dx.
This adds a small rectangular sliver of area.
The height of this sliver is exactly f(x).
Thus, the derivative of area is the height.
animations: Zoom into the right edge of the shaded area at x.
Add a thin rectangle of width dx (#FFD700) and height f(x).
Highlight the height f(x) with a vertical pink arrow (#FF00FF).
Show the equation dA/dx = f(x) in bright white (#FFFFFF).

sections.title: Formalizing the Relationship (FTC)
lecture_lines: This connection is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
To find an integral, find its antiderivative F.
The total area is the change in F.
We calculate this by subtracting F(a) from F(b).
Integration and differentiation are officially inverse processes.
animations: Display the integral symbol and equation ∫ f(x) dx (#FFFFFF).
Introduce the capital F(x) (#00FF00) as the 'Antiderivative'.
Show the subtraction F(b) - F(a) with blue arrows (#1E90FF) pointing to boundaries.
Flash the entire equation to emphasize the completed connection.

sections.title: Real-World Application: The Water Tank
lecture_lines: Imagine water flowing into a tank at rate f(t).
The flow rate is the derivative of volume.
Integrating this rate gives the total water volume.
animations: Show a leaking pipe [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/pipe.svg] (#A9A9A9) with water drops falling.
Show a bucket [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/bucket.svg] (#FFFFFF) filling with blue water (#0000FF) over time.
Plot a simple rate curve (#FF4500) and shade the area beneath it to show accumulation.

sections.title: Summary & Synthesis
lecture_lines: Differentiation breaks the area down into heights.
Integration sums heights to reconstruct the area.
They are two sides of one mathematical coin.
animations: Show a circular flow: f(x) -> Integrator -> F(x) in gold (#FFD700).
Show the reverse: F(x) -> Differentiator -> f(x) in silver (#C0C0C0).
Rotate the entire cycle to represent the inverse relationship.
